summary: The batch is safe on length and mostly kid-friendly, and its Commons and Uncommons are often well observed (boot hiding its partner, bowler hat rolling down the high street, hat-head, sock with a holey toe at a friend's house, socks-with-sandals grandad, shoelace losing its aglet, jeans pocket fluff). Above Uncommon, though, it falls back on formulas. About 90 Epics are crowd lines ('was worn by every X at Y, and the Z looked like…' / 'with every X at once') with a simile instead of a consequence, and about 90 Legendaries are longevity tallies ('has been worn for N years and still has its original…') with no outrageous achievement and no punchline. Most Rares describe the item doing its job ('Kept a climber's face warm') rather than a troublesome power. Together these mean roughly three of five rarities per object need rewriting. Names are misaligned in about 15 objects, often off by one (bathing cap, jeans, brassiere, headband, crown, tiara, helmet). Epic names are event titles, and Legendary names mostly follow one 'Lady/Sir/Madame X of the Y' shape. Near-duplicate objects share premises (two pyjamas, two swim trunks, maillot/swimsuit, robe/bathrobe, high heel/stiletto, cleats/football boot, balaclava/ski mask, bow/ribbon), and stock gags repeat (biscuit tin copied word for word, horses with earplugs, mirror polish, soup dipping, shrinking in the wash). Hard flags: Christmas in stockings E and L, church-coded vestment lines and 'Candle-Hot Procession', swimwear and underwear hints (kilt C, tights 'Crotchsag', maillot 'Wedgiewriggle', bikini C, swim trunks R, 'Nursery Blowout', 'Thong Strap Flick'), brand or character echoes (Old Flipper, Wedgewood, Golden Boot, Pyjamarama, Velveteen), and famous-person hooks. Move mechanics are mostly respected for legend moves (heal, buff, drain and ×3 names fit). The problems are about 18 garbled signature names ('Strap Snatch Snap Snap'), a 'Snatch' on boot's plain-hit signature, Ultimates that copy the Epic name (three exact copies), and variant Ultimates with effect-specific names ('Frozen Pond Spin' on a burn). Every high and medium issue carries a concrete replacement, and each new name is checked to be unique and within length limits.

patterns.pattern: Epic formula: 'Was worn by every X at Y, and the Z looked like…' or '… with every X at once'. Roughly 90 of 118 Epics use a crowd of identical items as the whole joke, usually ending in a simile (field of mushrooms, bowl of sweets, sea of tents, row of turtles) instead of a consequence.
patterns.suggestion: Give each Epic one object doing something huge with a concrete fallout (for example bucket hat: 'Flipped over at the festival and was used as a real bucket. It carried enough mud to build a second stage.'). Rotate mechanisms: physics (pool plug pulled, snow sliding off a roof), silly logistics (lunch on a stuck ski lift), literal misunderstanding (shoe tree grows into a tree). Per-object replacements are in the issues.

patterns.pattern: Legendary formula: 'Has been worn/walked/kept … for N years and still has its original X' (or 'never once …'). About 90 Legendaries are longevity or tally lines with no outrageous achievement and no punchline.
patterns.suggestion: Each Legendary needs one concrete, outrageous feat plus a deflating punchline (for example jeans: 'Went so long without a wash that they now stand in the corner on their own. Last week they went to the shops alone.'). Keep cosmic scale to about a third of the batch. Per-object replacements are in the issues.

patterns.pattern: Rares describe the item doing its normal job well ('Kept a skier's face warm', 'Gripped the muddiest pitch', 'Kept a farmer clean') instead of a troublesome power.
patterns.suggestion: Turn the function into a power with a cost to someone (for example sun hat: 'Follows the sun round the garden by itself, dragging its owner along. Grandpa has been round the house nine times today.').

patterns.pattern: Names sit on the wrong rarity (often off by one): for example bathing cap C/U swapped, jeans C 'Kneeripper' on the shrink line, brassiere names shifted one rarity, crown R 'Slidedown' on the cake line, tiara R 'Hairslipper' on the pigeon line, helmet R 'Helmethair'.
patterns.suggestion: Write each name after its own lore line. Each re-paired name is listed as its own issue (for example jeans: Common 'Shrinker', Rare 'Kneeripper').

patterns.pattern: Epic names are event or scene titles ('Swimming Pool Lap', 'Office Corridor Clatter', 'Sunday Lounge', 'Summer Heatwave'), not creatures; most of them also stop fitting once the Epic is rewritten.
patterns.suggestion: Use creature-like names tied to the new Epic (for example 'Plugpuller', 'Puddlequake', 'Shoe Orchard', 'Slugscarer').

patterns.pattern: Legendary names repeat one shape, 'Title X-ington of the Place' (Lady/Madame/Sir/Lord/Captain/Old … of the …), in about 90 of 118 names, against the tracker lesson to vary name shapes.
patterns.suggestion: Vary the shapes: plain epithet ('The Bottomless Overcoat', 'The Crown That Crowned a Cat'), name and deed ('Lady Bootella, Sea Strider', 'Old Buckleworth, Tower Holder'), or a single strong name. Keep 'of the …' for at most a quarter.

patterns.pattern: Signature moves: almost every Clothing signature is '<part> Snatch', and about 18 are garbled or doubled ('Brim Snatch Snatch', 'Strap Snatch Snap Snap', 'Strap Snatch Strap'), which also falsely suggests a multi-hit.
patterns.suggestion: Use one clean drain verb per object and vary it (tug, grab, yank, twang, pinch, borrow), for example 'Hat Grab', 'Tassel Tug', 'Elastic Twang'. Shoe signatures are plain hits and must not use 'Snatch' (boot).

patterns.pattern: Ultimates reuse the Epic monster name or its key words (roller shoe, shoe horn and snow boot are exact copies; many others are near copies such as 'Festival Field Bounce', 'Steamy Street Mystery', 'Corridor Clatter').
patterns.suggestion: Give each finisher its own image (for example 'Full Speed Wheelie', 'Big Slide-In', 'Big Fur Stomp', 'Case Closed').

patterns.pattern: Variant-dependent Ultimates whose names commit to one effect: cold words on burn variants ('Frozen Pond Spin', 'Snow Day Trudge'), 'Daze' on stun/defdown mixes, 'Smelly' on poison/stun, 'Barrage' or 'Lap After Lap' on single hits, cosy words on attacks ('Armchair Snuggle', 'Sofa Snuggle Heat').
patterns.suggestion: Use effect-neutral finisher names when variants differ (for example 'Showstopper Spin', 'Sock Surprise', 'Big Snowball', 'Big Button Pop').

patterns.pattern: Laundry and washing-machine premises are overused across the batch: shrinking (jeans C/E, wool R, crop top U, vest R), lost or tangled in the wash (socks C/E/L, brassiere C/R, underwear R/E, shirt U/E, pyjamas E, tights E).
patterns.suggestion: Keep at most one laundry premise per object and no more than about 6 in the batch; the replacements in the issues move the rest to other traits.

patterns.pattern: Near-duplicate objects reuse each other's premises: i_pajama / x_pajamas, i_swimming_trunks / x_swim_trunks, i_maillot / x_swimsuit, x_bathrobe / x_robe, x_high_heel / x_stiletto, x_cleats / x_football_boot, x_balaclava / i_ski_mask, x_bow / x_ribbon, i_breastplate / i_cuirass / i_chain_mail.
patterns.suggestion: Before writing each pair, list each object's premises side by side and give every pair its own angle (for example robe: door-hanging uncle and teabag pocket; bathrobe: trailing belt and fluffy hallway).

patterns.pattern: Repeated stock gags inside the batch: biscuit tin (nightgown R = slipper R word for word), 'horses wore earplugs' (chain mail E = cuirass E), mirror polish (breastplate U, cuirass U, brogue R, pump U), dipping in soup (tie C, lanyard C, vestment C, academic gown C), over-your-eyes Commons (bandana, bucket hat, fedora, headband, crown, onesie), squinting/sunglasses (crown U and E, badge R, sari R, tights R), 'still smells of sun cream' (sun hat L, sarong L).
patterns.suggestion: Use each gag once in the batch. The over-your-eyes Commons are left in place for bandana and fedora, but the writer should vary at least two more (for example bucket hat: 'Collects rain in its brim and pours it down your neck when you nod.').

patterns.pattern: Uncommons that are plain descriptions with no joke ('Is made of a thousand tiny metal rings', 'Is spun from a sheep's fleece', 'Has stretchy sides so you can slip it on', 'Zips up from your toes to your chin').
patterns.suggestion: Add the twist or attitude (for example chain mail: 'Catches every crumb in its rings. A knight can eat breakfast out of it at lunchtime.').

patterns.pattern: Taste, religion, brands and real people: Christmas stockings and a church-coded vestment; swimwear and underwear jokes that hint at exposure (kilt C, tights C, maillot C, bikini C, swim trunks R, 'Nursery Blowout', 'Thong Strap Flick'); brand or character echoes (Old Flipper, Wedgewood, Golden Boot, Velveteen, Pyjamarama, a grey wanderer's cloak; the croc object itself is a brand name, so keep 'Croc' out of names and lore); implied real people (a famous climber, a famous swimmer, a famous dancer, dinner with royalty).
patterns.suggestion: Apply the per-object replacements: secular framing for the vestment (town hall, not ceremony or candles), no Christmas in stockings, swimwear and underwear jokes about knots, colours, floating and laundry only, and no famous-person hooks.
